lead: This unit explains how operating systems protect resources and how security is enforced. After reading you will identify protection goals, describe access control mechanisms, and understand basic distributed security.
about: Unit 6 consists of nine chapters. Chapter 6.1 introduces protection goals and principles. Chapter 6.2 defines a protection domain. Chapter 6.3 presents the access matrix and its concrete forms. Chapter 6.4 covers access control policies and revocation. Chapter 6.5 looks at capability‑based and language‑based protection. Chapter 6.6 surveys common threats and attacks. Chapter 6.7 explains distributed operating systems and synchronization. Chapter 6.8 describes distributed file systems. Chapter 6.9 compares Linux and Windows security mechanisms. The chapters progress from abstract goals to concrete implementations and finally to real‑world examples.

chapters.idea: Define the main protection goals and the principles that guide their enforcement.
chapters.depth: Cover confidentiality, integrity, availability and accountability. Explain the principles of least privilege, fail‑safe defaults, open design and separation of duties. Mention that some syllabi call them security objectives or security policies.

figure.aria: Shows the three primary protection goals as nested items.

chapters.example: A mobile wallet app must keep the balance confidential (no other app can read it), ensure only the owner can debit (integrity), and stay operational during a power cut (availability).
chapters.trap: Mixing confidentiality with integrity – students often think a read‑only file also guarantees it cannot be altered.
chapters.leave: Detailed threat categorisation is covered in chapter 6.6.

chapters.idea: Introduce the concept of a protection domain that groups subjects, objects and rights.
chapters.depth: Explain subjects, objects, access rights and the reference monitor. Use the terms security domain or protection domain as some syllabi do. Only a few universities teach this in depth, so keep the description concise.

figure.title: Reference Monitor
figure.aria: Shows a subject asking the reference monitor for access to an object.

chapters.example: Process P1 (subject) asks to read file F1 (object). The reference monitor checks that P1 has read right in its domain.
chapters.trap: Confusing a protection domain with the access matrix – they are related but not the same.
chapters.leave: Implementation details of the matrix are in chapter 6.3.

chapters.idea: Model all access rights with an access matrix and show two practical implementations.
chapters.depth: Define the matrix with subjects as rows, objects as columns, and rights as entries. Describe Access‑Control Lists (ACLs) as column‑wise implementation and capability lists as row‑wise implementation. Called protection matrix in some courses.

figure.title: Access Matrix
figure.aria: Shows a 3×2 matrix where S1 can read object O1, S2 can write O2, and S3 can read O1 and write O2.

chapters.example: Three subjects S1‑S3 and two files O1, O2. The matrix entry (S1,O1)=R, (S2,O2)=W, (S3,O1)=R, (S3,O2)=W.
chapters.trap: Assuming the matrix must be stored completely in memory – real systems use ACLs or capabilities to avoid this.
chapters.leave: Revocation mechanisms are discussed in chapter 6.4.

chapters.idea: Explain how operating systems grant, check and revoke access rights.
chapters.depth: Cover discretionary and mandatory access control, role‑based access control, ACLs and capability revocation methods (invalidation, garbage collection). Some syllabi list these as access control policies and revocation techniques.

figure.aria: Shows the flow from a user request through the access control module to revocation and update of permissions.

chapters.example: User U loses admin role. The system removes write permission on file /etc/passwd by deleting the corresponding ACL entry.
chapters.trap: Thinking revocation instantly removes all previously distributed capabilities – copies may linger until garbage collected.
chapters.leave: Advanced capability delegation is covered in chapter 6.5.

chapters.idea: Present capability‑based protection and language‑based safety mechanisms.
chapters.depth: Describe unforgeable capability tokens, delegation, and revocation. Explain language‑based protection such as type safety, sandboxing and object‑capability model. Only a few universities teach this in detail, so keep it brief.

figure.aria: Shows capability delegation from App A to B and then to Service C.

chapters.example: A mobile payment app receives a payment‑token capability and passes it to a vendor app, which then uses it to call the bank service.
chapters.trap: Assuming a capability system prevents all programming bugs – it only controls authority, not logic errors.
chapters.leave: Threat analysis and attacks are discussed in chapter 6.6.

chapters.idea: List the main categories of threats and typical attacks on operating systems.
chapters.depth: Cover program threats (buffer overflow, injection), system threats (privilege escalation, rootkits), network threats (DoS, MITM) and basic cryptographic tools (hash, symmetric encryption). Some syllabi name these as attack vectors or security classifications.

figure.aria: Shows a tree with three top‑level threat categories and two example attacks under each.

chapters.example: If a service has a 1 % buffer‑overflow vulnerability and an exploit succeeds 50 % of the time, the overall attack success probability is 0.01 × 0.5 = 0.005 (0.5 %).
chapters.trap: Ignoring insider threats – many attacks originate from legitimate users.
chapters.leave: Defensive mechanisms are introduced in later chapters on distributed systems.

chapters.idea: Explain how a distributed OS provides transparency and how nodes synchronize actions.
chapters.depth: Define distributed operating system, transparency types (location, migration, replication) and synchronization primitives such as Lamport timestamps and distributed mutexes. Some syllabi refer to this as network OS or cluster OS.

figure.aria: Shows the exchange of messages for a distributed lock using a reference monitor.

chapters.example: Node1 sends a lock request with timestamp 5. RM checks Node2’s timestamp (7) and grants the lock to Node1. After the critical section Node2 releases its lock.
chapters.trap: Assuming a global clock exists – distributed algorithms rely on logical clocks instead.
chapters.leave: File‑system consistency is covered in chapter 6.8.

chapters.idea: Describe the architecture and consistency models of distributed file systems.
chapters.depth: Cover client‑server and peer‑to‑peer layouts, replication strategies, strong vs. eventual consistency, caching, and failure handling. Only a few universities teach the full replication protocols, so the description is concise.

figure.title: DFS Architecture
figure.aria: Shows a client accessing a local cache that synchronizes with two replicated servers.

chapters.example: A file is written on Server1. The system replicates it to Server2. A later read from the client may return stale data with probability 0.02 if replication delay is 200 ms.
chapters.trap: Assuming every operation is strongly consistent – many DFS use eventual consistency for performance.
chapters.leave: Real‑world implementations are examined in chapter 9.

chapters.idea: Compare how Linux and Windows implement protection and security features.
chapters.depth: Discuss Linux UID/GID, DAC, SELinux/AppArmor, capabilities, and sudo. For Windows, cover security identifiers (SID), ACLs, integrity levels, User Account Control (UAC) and token based access. Some syllabi label this as OS security architecture.

figure.aria: Shows two vertical stacks, one for Linux and one for Windows, listing their security layers.

chapters.example: Linux user creates file with mode 600 → only owner can read/write. Windows user creates file with ACL granting Read/Write to his SID only; UAC prompts when an admin tries to modify it.
chapters.trap: Treating Linux capabilities as identical to Windows privileges – they operate at different abstraction levels.
